title: AI strategy consulting: what should you walk away with?
description: What good AI strategy help leaves you with: one ranked workflow, a baseline, a 90-day plan and AI rules. Plus cost and free options.
verdict: Buy a decision, not a deck. Firms that redesign the work and measure impact get more from AI.[^14][^15]
Most AI stalls on people and process, not models.[^16][^11] So good strategy focuses on workflow, data and ownership.
People keep the calls: an executive owns AI risk; named staff check output.[^2] You're liable for what your AI says.[^7]
Set AI rules in week one: most AI users bring their own tools.[^28] List AI in use; write a policy.[^2]
Most mid-market firms, 70%, say they need outside help to get the most from AI.[^19][^20]

onPage.text: The five things good AI strategy help leaves you holding
Three ways the work can run, sized to your firm
Who US employers hire: people to build AI, or to own it
Why most AI pilots stall, and the fix for each
Eight checks to judge any AI advisor before you sign
When to skip strategy help, and what to use instead

summary: AI strategy consulting is outside help to decide where AI pays first, in what order and under what rules, before anyone builds. Good work ends in one ranked workflow, a baseline number and named owners.[^3][^15] Whether the work gets redesigned around AI makes or breaks it.[^15][^14]
walkAway: One ranked list of workflows, scored on value, data readiness, risk and owner, with the top one named.[^19] Firms with fewer failed AI projects weigh risk, compliance and data when they pick.[^27]

A baseline number for that workflow, measured before any tool is bought: hours, cycle time, error rate or cost.[^10][^3] High performers are twice as likely to have set ways to measure AI's impact.[^14]
A 90-day plan with an owner for each step and a go-or-stop date.[^15] Leaders need "the courage to exit experiments that are not delivering".[^22]
A governance baseline: an AI use policy, a list of the AI already in use, and who signs off.[^2] Of staff who use AI, 78% bring their own tools to work.[^28]
A written list of what not to do, and why each idea was cut.[^10] Chasing new technology instead of the problem is a common root cause of AI project failure.[^11]
humanRole: CEO or COO: owns decisions about AI risk.[^2] Firms whose CEO oversees AI governance report more bottom-line impact from AI.[^15]
Process owners (ops lead, controller, underwriter): pick the workflow and check AI output.[^2][^1] AI helps them work: support agents with an AI assistant resolved 15% more issues an hour.[^12]
A named person signs off anything AI tells customers. A tribunal held Air Canada liable for its chatbot's wrong fare advice, and rejected the claim the bot was separate.[^7]

People keep decisions about individuals, such as hiring, lending, insurance, housing and health care.[^5] Colorado's SB26-189 covers AI used to make, guide or assist those decisions, from 1 Jan 2027.[^5][^6]

recipes.name: 1. Owner-led firm, about 40 to 120 staff: one workflow first
recipes.when: The CEO still owns AI, there are many ideas and no data team. Winners "pick one pain point, execute well, and partner smartly".[^18][^17]
flow: CEO: name the three jobs that cost the most time or errors
Ops lead: time one of them for two weeks to get a baseline
Advisor: score the three on value, data, risk and owner
CEO: pick one and set a go-or-stop date
Team lead: run a 30-day pilot, with a person checking every AI output
CEO: go, change or stop on the date
recipes.cost: Free first pass: an SBDC advisor, or a subsidized Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP) center if you make things.[^9][^8] For paid help, ask for a fixed price and a fixed scope.

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size firm, about 120 to 500 staff: a ranked portfolio plus rules
recipes.when: Several division heads want AI, staff already use their own tools, and a board or lender wants a plan.[^28] Of mid-market AI users, 79% have a roadmap but only 37% call it well formed.[^20]
flow: COO: sponsor it; ask each division head for their two costliest jobs
IT or ops lead: list the AI tools already in use
Advisor: score the candidates and draft the AI use policy
Division heads: confirm a baseline for each candidate
COO: rank the top 2 or 3 and name an owner for each
CEO: sign off the 90-day plan and the policy
Owners: pilot at one site or team first, with a monthly review
recipes.cost: Ask for a fixed price and scope, with any build quoted separately. Zavient's own sprint, for example, runs a fixed 30 days.[^30]

recipes.name: 3. Firm where AI touches decisions about people: rules first
recipes.when: You lend, insure, hire or run health care, and AI already touches those decisions.[^5] Most executives lack strong confidence they'd pass an AI governance audit within 90 days.[^22]
flow: Compliance lead: list every AI system that touches a decision about a person
Advisor: map each one to the AI framework of NIST, the US standards body, and to state rules
Division head (e.g. head of lending): decide where a person must review
COO: approve the policy and how often it is reviewed
Then: run recipe 1 for the first value workflow
recipes.cost: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and its Playbook are free.[^1][^2] The international AI management standard, ISO/IEC 42001, costs CHF 225 to buy; certification is extra.[^4]

ownData.title: Are US employers hiring people to build AI, or to decide where it goes?
ownData.intro: We counted US job ads by job title, posted in the 30 days to 25 Nov 2026.[^31][^32] Builder titles drew about 56 ads for every ad for a head of AI or chief AI officer.[^31] So few firms hire an AI leader, and the call on where AI goes usually falls to the CEO or COO.[^31][^2]
ownData.note: Source: Zavient count of US job ads in the JobsPipe index, by title keyword, pulled 25 Nov 2026.[^31][^32] Counts are the provider's estimates, titles overlap, and "head of AI" can catch "head of AI engineering". All employer sizes are counted, and an ad is not a hire.

watchOuts: Wrong problem or wrong metric is RAND's most common root cause of failure.[^11] Fix: write down the business metric and its owner before picking a tool.
Data not ready: it is mid-market firms' top AI barrier, and Gartner expects most projects without AI-ready data to be dropped.[^21][^25] Fix: check the data on a real sample in week one.
Chasing the tech, not the problem: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by end of 2027.[^26][^11] Fix: first ask whether a rule, template or existing tool does the job.[^10]
Skipping people and process, where about 70% of AI challenges sit.[^16][^21] Fix: redesign the workflow with the team that does it, the biggest driver of profit from AI.[^15]
No baseline, so no proof: about a third of firms don't track AI value yet.[^36][^23] Fix: measure today's numbers before the pilot starts.
Trials with no end date: the average firm scrapped 46% of its AI proofs of concept (trial projects) before production.[^27][^24] Fix: set a go-or-stop date, and stop what misses it.[^22]
howToTest: Record today's numbers for one workflow for two weeks: volume, hours, errors and cycle time.[^10][^3]
Ask to see the scoring rubric, plus the scores of the ideas they cut.[^27]
Hold back 50 to 100 real past cases the advisor never sees, and try the advice on them. Benchmarks should mirror the real task, edge cases included.[^35][^37]
Compare it with the cheapest option: a rule, a template or an off-the-shelf tool. Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds.[^10][^17]
Try a hard case on purpose. On a task outside AI's reach, consultants using AI were 19 points less likely to be right.[^13]
Price the lift: hours saved times loaded hourly cost, minus the cost to run it. US private employers paid $46.89 per hour worked in June 2026; use your own pay data first.[^34]
Agree a stop rule and a date before the pilot starts.[^22] RAND advises picking problems you'd commit a team to for at least a year.[^11]
Check what they told you not to do, and why.[^10] Red flag: a deck with no named workflow, owner or stop date.
Get the rubric, scores, baseline and policy as files you keep, so the work outlives the engagement.

faq.q: What's the difference between AI strategy and AI automation consulting?
faq.a: Strategy decides what gets built, in what order and why; automation builds it and runs it. Our AI automation consulting guide covers the build. Either way, define the business value first, as NIST's AI framework asks.[^3]

faq.q: How much does AI strategy consulting cost?
faq.a: We found no neutral survey of AI strategy fees, so we give no range. Ask for a fixed price and a fixed scope, with any build quoted separately. For a first pass, SBDC advice is free and MEP centers are subsidized.[^9][^8]

faq.q: Is AI consulting actually worth it for small and mid-sized businesses?
faq.a: Only for a problem with a number attached: winners pick one pain point.[^18] Of middle-market firms, 70% say they need outside help to get the most from AI.[^19] A free SBDC advisor is a fair first step.[^9]

faq.q: How long does an AI strategy take?
faq.a: Weeks, not months, for a focused version. Zavient's fixed-scope sprint runs 30 days.[^30] Mid-market top performers went from pilot to full use in about 90 days, against nine months or more at large firms.[^17]

faq.q: What is an AI readiness assessment?
faq.a: A check of your strategy, data, governance, skills and infrastructure. Free vendor self-checks exist: Microsoft's takes about 45 minutes, and Cisco's covers six areas.[^33][^38] Gartner found 63% of data leaders lack or are unsure of AI-ready data practices.[^25]

faq.q: Who should own AI strategy at a mid-size company?
faq.a: A senior operator with budget, often the CEO or COO.[^2][^15] Few firms hire a dedicated AI leader: in our count, builder job ads outnumber AI-owner ads about 56 to 1.[^31]

pickElse: You already know the workflow, the data and the owner: skip strategy, and buy a tool or scope a build with automation help. Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about 67% of the time.[^17]
Under about 50 staff or on a tight budget: start with a free SBDC advisor, or an MEP center if you make things.[^9][^8] New York's MEP guide recommends a pilot-first approach.[^39]
You only need a governance baseline: use the free NIST AI RMF Playbook.[^2] Add ISO/IEC 42001 if customers ask for a certificate.[^4]
Staff just need to use AI well day to day: an approved tool plus training, not a strategy project.[^28] Most small-business owners (73%) say more training would help them put AI to work.[^29]

offer.heading: Not sure where AI pays first? Get a free 30-minute diagnostic
offer.body: Free, before any paid work: 30 minutes on your first workflow. Bring your three costliest jobs. You leave knowing which to start with, the number to track and what to skip.

reviews.notes: Would skip the job-ad table because the 'Other' label meant nothing; relabelled the column 'Counted as' with Builder, Owner or Neither. Wanted the strategy-versus-automation split early, so that FAQ now comes first. Recipe 2's cost now asks for a fixed price and scope, with any build quoted separately. No neutral fee range exists, so none is given.

Tripped on NIST and ISO/IEC 42001 with no explanation; both now say what they are on first use in recipe 3. 'Proofs of concept' read as jargon; now glossed as trial projects. Step flows name a role on every line and read fine on a phone.

Wanted to know if one site can go first; recipe 2's last step now pilots at one site or team. The job-ad numbers had no 'so what'; the intro now says the call on where AI goes usually falls to the CEO or COO. Pricing the lift in hours times loaded cost is the margin view a GM needs.

Read as the COO or head of operations who would hire the help. The eight checks work as a sales-call script; added a ninth: keep the rubric, scores, baseline and policy as your own files. Forum quotes were cut; the what-not-to-do item now rests on RAND and Google.

Steve wants a price and gets no fee range, since no neutral one exists, plus free SBDC and subsidized MEP routes; Zavient's own price is left out until the site owner approves it. The 'worth it' answer now leans on the pick-one-pain-point finding instead of a general rule. Recipe 1 fits a firm under about 120 staff, and the offer asks for his three costliest jobs, which he can bring cold.
